QF.id: IV Strategies Using Interest Rate Derivatives_18

question.text: A future borrower expects overnight MIBOR to rise from 6.25% to 6.75% over the next month. Using one standard exchange-traded Overnight MIBOR futures lot (notional Rs. 5 crore, one month, 30/365 basis), should the borrower go long or short MIBOR futures, and what is the approximate P&L?

answer.text: Go long MIBOR futures; profit approximately Rs. 20,550
Go short MIBOR futures; profit approximately Rs. 20,550
Go long MIBOR futures; profit approximately Rs. 1,370
Go short MIBOR futures; profit approximately Rs. 5,000

explanation.text: The Logic: A future borrower hedges rising short-term rates by going LONG Overnight MIBOR futures (workbook p. 161). The exchange-traded Overnight MIBOR futures contract is defined on notional principal of Rs. 5 crore for one month on a 30/365 basis, with a basis-point value of about Rs. 411 (workbook p. 121). For a 50 bp rise: P&L is approximately 50 x Rs. 411 = Rs. 20,550 per lot. The Trap: Going short would hedge falling rates, not rising rates. Rs. 1,370 uses a non-standard Rs. 1 crore one-day notional that is not the workbook contract. Rs. 5,000 uses an incorrect day-count adjustment. Note: A future borrower goes LONG Overnight MIBOR futures so the futures gain offsets the higher borrowing cost when rates rise.
